We proposed the role of locus of control (chance) and trait cynicism as antecedents of moral disengagement in the context of ethically minded consumer behavior. The relationship of moral disengagement (Bandura, 2016) with neutralization techniques (Sykes & Matza, 1957) is subsequently examined.

2.3 | The relationship between moral disengagement and neutralization techniques

Sykes and Matza (1957) devise five specific neutralization techniques, which include denial of responsibility, denial of injury, denial of the victim, condemnation of the condemners and appeal to higher loyalties. These are developed in the context of juvenile delinquency, and from a criminology perspective, these techniques describe how criminal activity is rationalized by offenders (Sykes & Matza, 1957).

In addition to moral disengagement (Bandura et al., 1996), prior research on unethical consumer behavior uses neutralization techniques proposed by Sykes and Matza (1957) to explain why consumers do not engage in ethical consumer behavior (or actively engage in unethical consumer behavior). Neutralization techniques (Sykes & Matza, 1957) are used to explain counterfeit consumption (Bian et al., 2016; Koay, 2018; Omeraki Çekirdekci & Baruonu Latif, 2019), digital piracy (Hinduja, 2007, 2018; Phau et al., 2016; Siponen et al., 2012), meat consumption (as opposed to vegetarianism, which is positively related to animal welfare, Dowsett et al., 2018), purchasing Fairtrade products (Brunner, 2014; Chatzidakis et al., 2007), non-green purchasing (Johnstone et al., 2015), deviant consumer behavior (Dootson et al., 2018; Harris & Daunt, 2011; Harris & Dumas, 2009; Rosenbaum et al., 2011), ethically questionable behavior (Fukukawa et al., 2017; Fukukawa et al., 2019) and the lack of sustainable consumer behavior (Gruber & Schlegelmilch, 2014).

Although both moral disengagement (Bandura et al., 1996) and neutralization techniques (Sykes & Matza, 1957) are used to explain unethical consumption, prior research does not clearly delineate or differentiate between these constructs. Furthermore, moral disengagement (Bandura et al., 1996) and neutralization techniques (Sykes & Matza, 1957) are not concurrently empirically examined in the same study on ethical consumer behavior. Some studies conceptualize these as similar or reflecting the same underlining construct (Kvalnes & Nordal, 2019; Ribeaud & Eisner, 2010). Kvalnes and Nordal (2019) use the term “moral neutralization” to explain how financial professionals psychologically justify their unethical business practices that led to the financial crisis in Iceland. Kvalnes and Nordal (2019) state that moral neutralization includes the five neutralization techniques developed by Sykes and Matza (1957). Kvalnes and Nordal (2019, p.765) also state that “processes of neutralization have also been discussed under headings of moral disengagement (Bandura, 1986; Bandura et al., 1996) …” Thus, Kvalnes and Nordal (2019), propose that moral disengagement and neutralization techniques are similar constructs.

It is appropriate to treat moral disengagement and neutralization techniques as separate constructs that differ in their level of abstractness and this is the approach adopted in this study. Moral disengagement refers to broad level processes that provide different general paths (behavior locus, agency locus, effects locus, and victim locus) for altering moral codes. These processes enable individuals to choose actions and behaviors that deviate from their moral standards without experiencing self-censure and guilt. Neutralization techniques are more specific mechanisms that enable individuals to engage in precise actions that are unethical. Moral

disengagement is relatively abstract whereas neutralization techniques are relatively concrete. This implies that consumers engaging in unethical consumer behavior (or avoid ethical consumer behavior), first employ the abstract processes of moral disengagement that provide the mental directions required to subsequently move to the concrete mechanisms of neutralization techniques. This enables them to engage in the relevant, precise unethical consumer behavior such as buying products that harm the environment. This reflects a sequential process whereby moral disengagement and neutralization techniques both have a role in unethical consumer behavior.

Other research in moral neutralization also allude to a multi-stage sequential path when individuals engage in unethical practices. Hakimi et al. (2020) refer to moral neutralization in the work environment to describe the process of nurses moving from ethical practice to moral indifference resulting from a discouraging work environment. This process moves through the stages of “feeling discouraged”, “normalization”, “giving up”, “becoming a justifier”, and “moral indifference” (Hakimi et al., 2020). Hakimi et al. (2020) do not specifically refer to moral disengagement (Bandura et al., 1996). However, they state that their findings have similarities with the neutralization techniques of Sykes and Matza (1957). Hakimi et al. (2020) propose that the “normalization” and “becoming a justifier” stages of moral neutralization coincide with some of the neutralization techniques of Sykes and Matza (1957). However, Sykes and Matza (1957) did not suggest a sequential process within their five neutralization techniques. Rather the suggested path in this study from moral disengagement to neutralization techniques explaining unethical consumer behavior reflects a sequential process. This proposed sequential path is discussed below.

Consumers who activate moral disengagement in the behavior locus (Bandura et al., 1996) in the context of consumption decisions are more likely to use detailed neutralization techniques to reinforce this moral restructure using mechanisms such as the denial of responsibility (one of the five neutralization techniques suggested by Sykes & Matza, 1957). For example, a consumer buying fast fashion products, which generally have negative environmental effects (Niinimäki et al., 2020) rather than buying more environmentally sustainable clothing, can use moral justification, a process of moral disengagement in the behavior locus (Bandura et al., 1996) to attach a worthy purpose to their purchase behavior. Consumers are likely to justify their choice by reasoning that fast fashion promotes social equality by providing access to trendy clothes for the masses, similar to the access affluent consumers have to designer clothing. This then enables denial of responsibility (a specific neutralization technique, Sykes & Matza, 1957) such as “it is not the responsibility of average consumers to reform the fast fashion industry, instead wealthier people should be paying for environmentally and socially sustainable clothing.” This leads to the following hypothesis:

H3a. Moral disengagement in the behavior locus is an antecedent to neutralization techniques that are used to avoid ethically minded consumer behavior.

Consumers who displace their responsibility in the moral disengagement agency locus (Bandura et al., 1996) when making consumption choices are likely to follow with detailed neutralization techniques that reinforce displaced blame or diffused responsibility to other stakeholders and hierarchical economic or social structures. For example, a consumer is likely to morally restructure through moral disengagement in the agency locus by placing blame for climate change on corporations by arguing that companies, and not consumers, are the largest emitters. Therefore, consumers have minimal responsibilities for climate change mitigation.

This can then be followed with an appeal to higher loyalties (a specific neutralization technique, Sykes & Matza, 1957) such as, “my responsibility is for my family first and society later. It is big business who is responsible for solving climate change.” This leads to the following hypothesis:

H3b. Moral disengagement in the agency locus is an antecedent to neutralization techniques that are used to avoid ethically minded consumer behavior.

The effects locus of moral disengagement (Bandura et al., 1996) minimizes harmful consequences. Consumers using moral disengagement in the effects locus follows this with precise justifications that reduce the perceived harm such as denial of injury (a specific neutralization technique, Sykes & Matza, 1957). For example, when purchasing from a retailer known to underpay their staff, the consumer is likely to initially diminish the negative outcomes by arguing that people are not substantially affected, and they are lucky to have employment. The consequences of their purchases are excused by constructing a narrative about how high the minimum wage is so there is no injury incurred by paying workers below the minimum wage. This leads to the following hypothesis:

H3c. Moral disengagement in the effects locus is an antecedent to neutralization techniques that are used to avoid ethically minded consumer behavior.

In the victim locus of moral disengagement (Bandura et al., 1996) human qualities are taken from victims of unethical behavior so that they are easily perceived as responsible for their circumstances or are not considered when assessing the negative consequences of the unethical action. For example, when deciding not to pay more for Fairtrade brands that pay workers a living wage, consumers are likely to use moral disengagement in the victim locus to argue that workers are not necessarily entitled to better living conditions. This is because they are accustomed to a life of hardship unlike middle or upper-class consumers. This can then be followed with specific justifications of denial of responsibility (a specific neutralization technique, Sykes & Matza, 1957) such as, “it is not my responsibility to purchase Fairtrade products because I cannot afford them” (Brunner, 2014). This leads to the following hypothesis:

H3d. Moral disengagement in the victim locus is an antecedent to neutralization techniques that are used to avoid ethically minded consumer behavior.

Table 1 provides the various moral disengagement processes and the corresponding neutralization techniques that are used in relation to unethical consumer behavior.

2.4 | Effects of locus of control (chance) and trait cynicism on ethically minded consumer behavior

Moral disengagement is used to explain how consumers engage in unethical consumer behavior (Chowdhury & Fernando, 2014; Egan et al., 2015) and avoid ethical consumption (Peeters et al., 2015; Sharma & Paço, 2021). Locus of control is identified as an antecedent to moral disengagement (Detert et al., 2008). Recall that we extend this to all four different loci of moral disengagement in the context of unethically minded consumer behavior. When making

As proposed earlier, the activation of moral disengagement in each of these loci leads consumers to employ specific neutralization techniques, enabling them to avoid ethically minded consumer behavior or engage in unethically minded consumer behavior. In relation to unethically minded consumer behavior, there exists a path from locus of control (chance) to moral disengagement (in the four different loci) to neutralization techniques leading to the avoidance of ethically minded consumer behavior or engagement in unethically minded consumer behavior. H4c. Moral disengagement in the effects locus and neutralization techniques sequentially mediate the effects of locus of control (chance) on ethically minded consumer behavior.

H4d. Moral disengagement in the victim locus and neutralization techniques sequentially mediate the effects of locus of control (chance) on ethically minded consumer behavior.

Similar to locus of control (chance), trait cynicism is identified as an antecedent to moral disengagement (Detert et al., 2008). In this study, we extend to all four different loci of moral disengagement in the context of unethically minded consumer behavior. When making consumption decisions with ethical implications, cynical consumers are likely to activate moral disengagement in the behavior, agency, effects, and victim loci. As proposed earlier, the activation of moral disengagement in each of these loci leads to the use of specific neutralization techniques to avoid ethically minded consumer behavior or engage in unethically minded consumer behavior. In relation to unethically minded consumer behavior, there is a path from trait cynicism to moral disengagement (in the four different loci) to neutralization techniques leading to the avoidance of ethically minded consumer behavior or engagement in unethically minded consumer behavior. Hence, moral disengagement and neutralization techniques are sequential mediators of the effects of trait cynicism on ethically minded consumer behavior. This leads to the following hypotheses:

H5a. Moral disengagement in the behavior locus and neutralization techniques sequentially mediate the effects of trait cynicism on ethically minded consumer behavior.

H5b. Moral disengagement in the agency locus and neutralization techniques sequentially mediate the effects of trait cynicism on ethically minded consumer behavior.

H5c. Moral disengagement in the effects locus and neutralization techniques sequentially mediate the effects of trait cynicism on ethically minded consumer behavior.

H5d. Moral disengagement in the victim locus and neutralization techniques sequentially mediate the effects of trait cynicism on ethically minded consumer behavior.

The conceptual model of the hypotheses is presented in Figure 1.

An online survey of US consumers is conducted to test the proposed hypotheses. A crosssectional research design is used as trait cynicism (Roberts & Zigarmi, 2014) and locus of control (Rotter, 1966), which are key constructs in this study, are predominantly dispositional. Hence, they are difficult to rapidly or easily manipulate in experimental settings. Prior research examining the antecedents of moral disengagement also uses cross-sectional designs (Detert et al., 2008).

3.1 | Sample

A total of 436 US adult consumers (49.54% male; 49.54% female; 0.91% others; mean age 44.9 years) are recruited from a consumer panel affiliated with Qualtrics. Qualtrics is an American-based market research company that is widely used in marketing and consumer research (e.g., Chowdhury, 2019; Chowdhury, 2020; Hoffmann & Plotkina, 2021).

3.2 | Measures

Participants provide responses to scales measuring the key constructs. Locus of control (chance) is measured with an eight-item scale developed by Levenson (1981). The items are assessed with a six-point Likert scale. The mean of the eight items reflects the participant's locus of control (chance). Trait cynicism is assessed with a five-item scale adapted from Chowdhury and Fernando (2014). Agreement with the items is measured with a seven-point Likert scale. The mean of the five items reflects the participant's trait cynicism.

A 24-item scale is used to measure moral disengagement. This scale is developed by Detert et al. (2008), modified from the work of Bandura et al. (1996). There are nine items for the behavior loci; six items for the agency loci; three items for the effects loci; and six items for the victim loci of moral disengagement (Detert et al., 2008). A seven-point Likert scale measures agreement with each item. The mean of the relevant items for each locus of moral disengagement is calculated to reflect the moral disengagement level of participants in the behavior, agency, effects, and victim loci respectively. Neutralization techniques are measured with the scale utilized by Fukukawa et al. (2017), which includes one item for each of the five neutralization techniques (Sykes & Matza, 1957). Agreement with the items is measured with a sevenpoint Likert scale. The mean of the five items reflects a participant's use of neutralization techniques.

A 10-item scale developed by Sudbury-Riley and Kohlbacher (2016) is used to assess ethically minded consumer behavior. A five-point Likert scale is used for recording responses to these items. The mean of the 10 items reflects a participant's ethically minded consumer behavior. Participants also provide responses to demographic questions in relation to age and gender.

The descriptive statistics (means and standard deviations) of the key variables are provided in Table 2. The correlations between the key variables are provided in Table 3.

3.3 | Validity and reliability

Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) is conducted using SPSS AMOS. A measurement model is tested with the items for locus of control (chance), trait cynicism, moral disengagement, neutralization techniques, and ethically minded consumer behavior loading on their respective factor. This enabled the assessment of the psychometric properties of the scales. Factor loadings reveal the following scale have factor loadings of <0.50, which is below the acceptable cut-off (Hair et al., 2010); three items from locus of control (chance), and one item each from moral disengagement behavior locus, moral disengagement agency locus and ethically minded consumer behavior. Accordingly, these items are deleted from their respective scales. The CFA reveals acceptable model fit (SRMR = 0.050; RMSEA = 0.056; CFI = 0.911). The average variance extracted (AVE) for all the scales are >0.45, which is the minimum prescribed level (Netemeyer et al., 2003). Heterotrait-monotrait (HTMT) ratio of correlations is used to assess discriminant validity (Henseler et al., 2015). All HTMT ratios are below the recommended level of 0.85. The Cronbach alphas of all scales are >0.70, which is the minimal acceptable level (Nunnally, 1978).

4 | RESULTS

4.1 | Relationship between locus of control (chance) and trait cynicism with moral disengagement

Four separate linear regressions are conducted to test the relationships between locus of control (chance) and trait cynicism with the four different loci of moral disengagement. These regressions test Hypotheses 1a–1d and Hypotheses 2a–2d. The following models reflect the regression analyses:

Gender (0 = male, 1 = non-male) and age are included in the regression models as covariates as prior research demonstrates they may affect ethical behavior (Bray et al., 2011; Dhir et al., 2021; Egan et al., 2015; Zaikauskaitė et al., 2022). Since age may have a non-linear effect, age2 is included to test for the slope of the age variable.

To assess multicollinearity, the VIF and tolerance values are examined for all variables in the regression models. All VIF values are less than five and all tolerance values are greater than 0.2 (except for those of age and age2, which are correlated). Hence multicollinearity is not likely to be a critical issue (Thompson et al., 2017).

The results of the four regression models are provided in Tables 4–7. Findings support hypotheses H1a, H1b, H1c and H1d as shown in Tables 4–7, demonstrate

that consumers who have a higher locus of control (chance) are more likely to morally disengage in the behavior locus, the agency locus, the effects locus, and the victim locus. Further-more, consumers who have higher trait cynicism are more likely to use moral disengagement in the victim locus. This supports H2d. However, as shown in Tables 4–7, H2a, H2b, and H2c are not supported, indicating consumers who have higher trait cynicism are not more likely to use moral disengagement in the behavior locus, agency locus or effects locus. The findings also demonstrate a significant role for gender. Males are more likely to use moral disengagement in all four loci. However, there is no significant association between age and moral disengagement.

Gender (0 = male, 1 = non-male) and age are also included in the regression model as covariates consistent with the previous analyses. Since age may have a non-linear effect, age2 is included to test for the slope of the age variable. The results of the regression analysis are provided in Table 8.

As shown in Table 8, findings support H3a. Moral disengagement in the behavior locus is positively related to the use of neutralization techniques. Similarly, moral disengagement in the victim locus is positively related to the use of neutralization techniques. Hence, H3d is also supported. However, there is no significant relationship between moral disengagement in the agency locus and moral disengagement in the effects locus with the utilization of neutralization techniques. Hence, H3b and H3c are not supported (see Table 8). There is no effect of gender or age in any of the models.

4.3 | Sequential mediation between locus of control (chance) and ethically minded consumer behavior

A mediation analysis is conducted using Model 80 of the PROCESS macro in SPSS (Hayes, 2017) to assess whether the various loci of moral disengagement (behavior, agency, effects, and victim) followed by neutralization techniques sequentially mediate the relationship between locus of control (chance) and ethically minded consumer behavior. In this mediation model, indirect effects of locus of control (chance) on ethically minded consumer behavior through the various loci of moral disengagement and neutralization techniques are estimated using bootstrapping (n = 5000). the mediation model. This tests H4a and H4b. The results of this mediation analysis are provided in Table 9.

The results demonstrate that moral disengagement in the behavior locus and neutralization techniques sequentially mediate the effects of locus of control (chance) on ethically minded consumer behavior. This supports H4a. Similarly moral disengagement in the victim locus and neutralization techniques sequentially mediate the effects of locus of control (chance) on ethically minded consumer behavior. This supports H4d. There are no sequential mediation effects through moral disengagement in the agency locus and neutralization techniques, or through moral disengagement in the effects locus and neutralization techniques. Hence, H4b and H4c are not supported.

The results also demonstrate an indirect effect of locus of control (chance) on ethically minded consumer behavior through moral disengagement in the agency locus. This indirect effect is positive and does not include any role of neutralization techniques.

4.4 | Sequential mediation between trait cynicism and ethically minded consumer behavior

A separate mediation analysis is conducted using Model 80 of the PROCESS macro in SPSS (Hayes, 2017) to assess whether the various loci of moral disengagement (behavior, agency, effects, and victim) followed by neutralization techniques sequentially mediate the relationship between trait cynicism and ethically minded consumer behavior. In this mediation model, indirect effects of trait cynicism on ethically minded consumer behavior through the various loci of moral disengagement and neutralization techniques are estimated using bootstrapping (n = 5000). Locus of control (chance), age, and gender are included as covariates in the mediation model. This tests H5a and H5b. The results of this mediation analysis are provided in Table 10.

5 | DISCUSSION

5.1 | Theoretical implications

In terms of theoretical contributions, the findings of this research demonstrate that moral disengagement and neutralization techniques are separate constructs that sequentially mediate the effects of locus of control (chance) and trait cynicism on ethically minded consumer behavior. These findings extend prior research in moral psychology (Bandura et al., 1996) and criminology (Sykes & Matza, 1957) on understanding the psychological processes that allow individuals to engage in unethical actions. In the context of unethical consumption, both moral disengagement and neutralization techniques are used. These are conceptually and empirically separate constructs that are used sequentially by consumers to avoid ethical consumer behavior or engage in unethical consumer behavior. This is different from other research that proposes that moral disengagement and neutralization techniques are very similar and can be subsumed under the term “moral neutralization” (Kvalnes & Nordal, 2019; Ribeaud & Eisner, 2010). Fur-thermore, the findings that both moral disengagement and neutralization techniques are sequentially used by consumers in unethical consumption contexts also distinguishes this research from other studies on unethical consumer behavior. These studies have either examined the role of moral disengagement (Chowdhury & Fernando, 2014; Sharma & Paço, 2021) or

the role or neutralization techniques (Bian et al., 2016; Brunner, 2014; Fukukawa et al., 2019; Phau et al., 2016), but have not examined these constructs concurrently.

The findings also reveal differential effects for the four different loci (behavior, agency, effects and victim loci) of moral disengagement. All four loci of moral disengagement are positively related to neutralization techniques. However, in relation to the effects of locus of control (chance) on ethically minded consumer behavior, moral disengagement in the behavior locus and victim locus are sequential mediators with neutralization techniques. Moral disengagement in the agency locus and in the effects locus are not mediators of the effects of locus on control (chance). In relation to the effects of trait cynicism on ethically minded consumer behavior, moral disengagement in victim locus is a sequential mediator with neutralization techniques. Moral disengagement in the behavior, agency and effects loci are not mediators of the effects of trait cynicism. Prior research on the role of moral disengagement in unethical consumer behavior (Chowdhury & Fernando, 2014; Sharma & Paço, 2021) has generally neglected the different roles of the various loci of moral disengagement.

Similar to Detert et al. (2008), this research shows that locus of control (chance) and trait cynicism are antecedents to moral disengagement, which subsequently leads to neutralization techniques and unethically minded consumer behavior. Consumers who believe that fate or luck decide their futures are more likely to use reconstructive mechanisms to explain away their less ethical behavior. Additionally, consumers who are inherently cynical distrust the good intent of other consumers or organizations and this leads to a feeling that any ethical contribution on the individual's part may be thwarted by these other entities.

However, our research contrasts with Detert et al. (2008) and extends it in the following ways. First, we examine the variables in an ethical consumption context as opposed to an organizational context. Second, our research shows that the various loci of moral disengagement have different roles in explaining the effects of locus of control (chance) and trait cynicism on unethical behavior. Furthermore, we illustrate the pivotal role of neutralization techniques subsequent to moral disengagement in relation to the effects of locus of control (chance) and trait cynicism; Detert et al. (2008) did not examine the role of neutralization techniques.

Additionally, an interesting finding of this research is that moral disengagement in the agency locus influences ethically minded consumer behavior positively for consumers with higher locus of control (chance). This paradoxical finding suggests that ethical consumer behavior is encouraged through eliciting a compassionate response. In this scenario, consumers assign agency to themselves instead of other reference group members (such as other consumers) or stakeholders (like businesses) when they perceive these groups or stakeholders as incapable of aiding themselves or others by engaging in ethical consumer behavior. Since the actions of the individual in the agency locus is influenced by the situations of others, this finding is supported by social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1986, 2007), which views society as an integrated part of an individual's identity. Thus, the level of agency or responsibility at the individual level is an important driver of ethically minded consumer behavior, including comparisons to the ability and responsibility of other stakeholders. This finding, that one of the loci of moral disengagement can be morally engaging in certain contexts such as ethical consumption, is novel and important.

5.2 | Practical contributions

At a practical level, the results are important for public policy makers and managers of firms

and victim locus of moral disengagement play key roles in mediating the effects of locus of control (chance) and trait cynicism on ethically minded consumer behavior. Hence communication campaigns should target consumers by counteracting moral disengagement, particularly the behavior and victim locus of moral disengagement. The behavior locus of moral disengagement can be counteracted through campaign messages that reinforce personal moral imperatives that align with social norms and highlight realistic comparisons that are difficult to mentally manipulate. The victim locus of moral disengagement can be counteracted by campaign messages that highlight the value of both human and nonhuman (e.g., other species and the environment) victims of unethical consumer behavior and attach greater personal responsibility to the consequences of unethical consumption.

Since the agency locus of moral disengagement is positively related to ethically minded consumer behavior, communication campaigns can also be developed to support the use of the agency locus. For example, campaign messages can show other individuals in consumption situations where they are incapable to engage in ethically minded consumer behavior (e.g., less affluent or vulnerable consumers may be financially or practically unable to engage in recycling and donation programs) so that individuals can take action and do the good that others cannot do.

Communication campaigns alone are unlikely to be effective in deterring unethical consumer behavior or encouraging ethical consumer behavior. The findings also provide insights for action from regulators. For example, policy may be introduced that restricts marketers' use of misleading euphemistic labelling such as big tobacco companies using ‘vapes’ instead of ‘e-cigarettes’.

Given that locus of control (chance) is an antecedent of moral disengagement, efforts can be made to empower consumers. This can be achieved by persuading consumers to believe in their ability to effect change through ethical actions, instead of yielding to fatalism and accepting socially and environmentally detrimental behavior. Similarly, as trait cynicism is an antecedent of moral disengagement, cynical consumers may be shown that, in many instances, people and firms do the good that they promise. Locus of control (chance) and trait cynicism are predominantly dispositional. Thus, short term or one-off campaigns may not be effective in counteracting their effects. Rather a longer-term process of educating consumers with high locus of control (chance) or cynical consumers is required.

Overall, this research contributes to better-informed consumers, marketers, and policymakers. This is consistent with recent industry trends and evolving consumer behaviors. Environmental, social, and governance strategies are increasingly being enforced at the company level, citing the need to meet community expectations (Bradley, 2023; Mohr et al., 2001). Global environmental and social trends such as alternatives to single-use products to reduce waste, advocacy for clean cities and carbon-free living, and inclusivity for all are reported to be key influences in consumers' purchasing intentions (Cromwell et al., 2023; Gaudig et al., 2021). This research provides insights to develop effective, tangible tools that can result in increased market share for ethical goods and services. This contributes to the future sustainability of the environment, economies, and societies in general. Finally, greater participation of consumers in ethically minded consumer behavior also has positive effects on consumer welfare as ethical consumption enhances consumer well-being (Ganglmair-Wooliscroft & Wooliscroft, 2019; Parvatiyar & Sheth, 2023).

6 | LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE RESEARCH

The research is based on a cross-sectional survey conducted at a specific point in time. Moral

(Bandura et al., 1975; Chatzidakis et al., 2007; Fukukawa et al., 2019; Sharma & Paço, 2021). Hence, by examining moral disengagement and neutralization techniques only as pre-pur-chase/pre-consumption mechanisms, this study may not provide a complete understanding of these complex psychological process. Although this research focuses on the psychological processes that precede unethical consumer behavior it does not rule out that moral disengagement, and neutralization techniques may also occur post-purchase/post-consumption and can potentially act to entrench ongoing unethical consumer behavior. Future research can examine the use of moral disengagement and neutralization techniques in post-purchase/post-consumption contexts. This would provide valuable insights. Furthermore, future research should focus on how the positive moral engagement effects of the agency locus of moral disengagement can be embedded in consumer behavior over time.

Another limitation of this research is that, unlike the four separate loci of moral disengagement, neutralization techniques are examined as a unidimensional construct. Specific neutralization techniques are not examined to identify which internal narratives are most frequently used following moral disengagement. Subsequent studies could explore the specific roles played by distinct neutralization techniques. Future research would also benefit from additional control variables that are related to ethical consumer behavior, such as spirituality and moral identity (Casidy & Arli, 2018; Chowdhury & Fernando, 2013; Rodriguez-Rad & Ramos-Hidalgo, 2018).

Finally, social desirability bias is a possibility with surveyed respondents potentially overstating their desire to be more ethical or “do the right thing” (Casais & Faria, 2022). A positive aspect of this research is that instead of measuring only self-reported attitudes and intentions, the ethically minded consumer behavior scale used in this study (Sudbury-Riley & Kohlbacher, 2016) measures self-reported behaviors. However, social desirability bias is not accounted for in this research, and future studies on ethically minded consumer behavior should control for the potential of social desirability bias.

# The Moral Credential Effect: When Good Deeds License Bad Behavior in Organizations

Association for Computing Machinery

Sarah, a senior engineering manager at a prominent tech company, had just finished leading a successful diversity recruitment initiative that increased female engineering hires by 40%. The program earned her recognition from the CEO and a company award for advancing inclusion. Two weeks later, during performance reviews, Sarah evaluated two equally qualified candidates for promotion: Marcus, an African American engineer, and Tom, a white engineer. Despite their comparable achievements, Sarah recommended Tom, rationalizing that Marcus “might not be ready for the increased pressure.” When a colleague questioned this decision, Sarah dismissed the concern, stating, “I've done more for diversity than anyone in this department. I know bias when I see it, and this isn't it.”

This scenario exemplifies the moral credential effect in action. Sarah's recent diversity work became a psychological license that paradoxically enabled discriminatory behavior. Her past good deeds served as credentials that, in her mind, proved she couldn't be biased, making her less vigilant about fairness in subsequent decisions.

Understanding the Moral Credential Effect

The moral credential effect occurs when individuals' past moral behavior paradoxically increases their likelihood of engaging in morally questionable actions. First formally identified by Monin and Miller in 2001, this phenomenon reveals how establishing oneself as unprejudiced can subsequently license expression of prejudiced attitudes \[1\]. Past good behavior creates a credit balance in one's moral account, which individuals unconsciously draw upon to justify later transgressions.

This bias manifests particularly strongly in organizational contexts involving diversity, ethics, and social responsibility. When individuals or organizations establish moral credentials through conspicuous ethical actions, they often become less careful about subsequent decisions, believing their established reputation provides immunity from moral scrutiny.

Empirical Evidence

In Monin and Miller's seminal study, participants who first disagreed with blatantly sexist statements were subsequently more willing to indicate that a stereotypically male job was better suited for men than women \[1\]. This foundational research has been replicated and extended across numerous contexts.

Effron, Cameron, and Monin demonstrated that individuals who endorsed Barack Obama were subsequently more likely to favor white job candidates over equally qualified Black candidates. Participants who had the opportunity to endorse Obama allocated prestigious job positions to white candidates at significantly higher rates than control groups \[2\]. If Sarah had publicly supported diversity candidates in previous hiring rounds, this research suggests she would be even more susceptible to bias in her evaluation of Marcus.

In consumer behavior, Mazar and Zhong found that people who purchased green products were subsequently more likely to lie and steal in laboratory experiments compared to those who purchased conventional products \[3\]. This “licensing effect” extends from environmental choices to ethical behavior, demonstrating the domain-crossing nature of moral credentials.

Khan and Dhar's research revealed that mere intent to perform good deeds can trigger licensing effects. Participants who imagined donating to charity were subsequently more likely to choose luxury items over utilitarian products \[4\]. This finding suggests that Sarah's planning of future diversity initiatives might further strengthen her credentialing bias.

A meta-analysis by Blanken, van de Ven, and Zeelenberg examining 91 studies with over 7,000 participants confirmed the robustness of moral licensing across diverse contexts, with an overall effect size of d = 0.31 \[5\]. The analysis revealed stronger effects when the licensing behavior was in the same domain as the subsequent questionable action.

Mechanisms and Origins: Why Good Deeds Go Bad

The moral credential effect emerges from fundamental psychological processes involving self-concept maintenance. According to self-completion theory, when people establish credentials in one domain, they feel less need to prove themselves in that area subsequently \[6\].

Merritt, Effron, and Monin proposed a moral credits model where good deeds function like deposits in a moral bank account \[7\]. Sarah's diversity initiative created a substantial deposit, which she unconsciously drew upon when making the biased promotion decision. Her internal dialogue might have been: “I've already proven I support diversity, so this decision must be based on merit alone.”

Research by Cascio and Plant demonstrated that moral credentials operate through reduced negative affect when engaging in potentially prejudiced behavior \[8\]. Individuals with established credentials experience less guilt or discomfort when making biased decisions, removing an important psychological barrier to discrimination.

Bradley et al. found that moral credentialing effects are amplified when credentials are publicly recognized \[9\]. Sarah's public award for diversity work would strengthen her licensing effect compared to private good deeds. The external validation reinforces internal justifications for subsequent bias.

Organizational Implications

Kaiser et al. discovered that the mere presence of diversity structures in organizations can create a “illusion of fairness” that licenses discrimination \[10\]. In studies across multiple companies, employees at organizations with diversity programs were less likely to perceive discrimination even when it objectively occurred.

Consider how this might affect Sarah's organization. The company's visible diversity initiatives create an organizational credential that makes both Sarah and her colleagues less likely to recognize bias in promotion decisions. The diversity program becomes a shield against scrutiny rather than a tool for change.

Castilla's field study of a large service organization found that implementing a merit-based reward system paradoxically increased gender and racial disparities in bonuses \[11\]. Managers who believed they were operating within an objective, fair system showed greater bias, suggesting that organizational credentials for fairness can license individual discrimination.

Practical Interventions: Disrupting the Credentialing Cycle

Organizations can implement evidence-based strategies to mitigate moral credentialing effects:

Continuous Monitoring and Feedback

Research by Monin and Miller suggested that making people aware of moral licensing can reduce its effects \[1\]. If Sarah's organization implemented regular bias audits with feedback, she might recognize her susceptibility to moral credentialing. Pope, Price, and Wolfers demonstrated that awareness of racial bias in NBA refereeing led to significant reductions in discriminatory calls \[12\].

Emphasizing consistency rather than balance

Conway and Peetz found that framing ethical behavior as reflecting core values rather than balanced choices reduced licensing effects \[13\]. Sarah's organization could emphasize that each decision reflects organizational values rather than allowing past good deeds to offset current choices.

Structured Decision Making

Uhlmann and Cohen showed that requiring justification for decisions before knowing the demographic characteristics of candidates reduced bias \[14\]. If Sarah had to document promotion criteria before reviewing candidate names, her credentialing bias would have less room to operate.

Accountability Partners

Tetlock's research on accountability demonstrates that knowing one must justify decisions to others reduces biased judgment \[15\]. Pairing Sarah with a colleague who reviews promotion decisions could disrupt credentialing effects through external accountability.

Replacing Retroactive with Prospective Framing

Zhang, Savani, and Morris found that focusing on future commitments rather than past achievements reduces moral licensing \[16\]. Sarah's organization could frame diversity work as an ongoing commitment rather than a past accomplishment, maintaining vigilance against bias.

Conclusion: Vigilance Against Virtue

The moral credential effect reveals how Sarah's genuine commitment to diversity paradoxically enabled discriminatory behavior. Her past good deeds became a license for present bias, illustrating a fundamental challenge in organizational ethics.

Recognition of this bias demands reconsidering how organizations approach diversity and ethics. Rather than celebrating achievements, organizations must maintain constant vigilance. Sarah's story reminds us that those most confident in their lack of bias may be most susceptible to it.

Success requires systematic approaches that assume human fallibility. Only through continuous monitoring, structured decisions, and cultural humility can organizations prevent moral credentials from undermining the very goals they represent. In ethics, as Sarah's case demonstrates, our greatest vulnerability comes not from recognized prejudice but from unexamined virtue.
